note: Mouse and plant studies, not human results.

cards.headline: Bones need gravity
cards.fact: Mice that spent 37 days on the space station lost bone in the thigh bone, which holds up the body's weight on Earth. Scientists think bones that carry weight are the ones that weaken when there is no gravity pushing on them.

cards.headline: Heads grow, legs shrink
cards.fact: In a 15-day shuttle flight, the skull bone of mice grew a little, even though leg bones normally get weaker in microgravity.

cards.headline: Tiny doses of radiation
cards.fact: Scientists gave mice small doses of three kinds of radiation, then checked their spleens 1, 2 and 4 months later.

cards.headline: Plants in zero gravity
cards.fact: On Earth, gravity tells roots and shoots which way to grow. Scientists flew Arabidopsis seeds to the ISS to see how they grow for 3 days with no gravity.

cards.headline: Roots in orbit
cards.fact: Arabidopsis seedlings grew for 12 days on the ISS, and their leaves and roots changed their proteins in different ways.

cards.headline: Plants that adapt
cards.fact: A plant with one gene changed had a much smaller gene response to spaceflight, so changing a plant's genes may help it adapt to space.

cards.headline: Strong muscles in space
cards.fact: In a spaceflight study, mice that got a treatment blocking two proteins called myostatin and activin A (which help limit muscle size) were protected against muscle and bone loss.
